cue: Almost no colour, a softer picture than yours, and eyes built for dim water.

cpd.note: a humpback whale's estimated sharpness stands for the group; seals measure higher and a manatee lower

fov.note: each side of a dolphin's head sees 120 to 130 degrees and the two eyes overlap by 20 to 30 degrees, so 2 x 125 - 25 = 225 degrees together

gain.note: half a log unit of extra dim-light sensitivity in a bottlenose dolphin, worked out as ten to the power 0.5

M.note: one kind of cone, tuned to long wavelengths, stands for whales and seals

sheen.note: records say a reflective layer is present in many species, but give no strength

SEA_L.note: the long-wavelength cone peak reported for dolphins and porpoises; the mapping to the picture is the app's

k.note: how strongly a heard sound draws rings across the picture

sound.name: rings
sound.note: sounds the microphone hears draw rings, as an echo might

rows: Dolphins, porpoises and seals have a single kind of cone, tuned to long wavelengths, and no blue-sensitive cone. In dolphins and porpoises that cone peaks near 523 nanometres. This view draws the picture with a single colour sensor, so colours collapse into lighter and darker shades.

Baleen whales and sperm whales have lost the genes for their cone pigments and rely on rods alone. A manatee has two kinds of cone, and a California sea lion picked out colours in behaviour tests. The single sensor picture is a middle case for the group.

A humpback whale resolves about 3.95 cycles per degree and a Bryde's whale 4.8. A false killer whale, a Pacific white-sided dolphin and a beluga managed 2.6 to 3.3. A harbour seal reaches 11.5 under water and a manatee only 1.6. Most of these values are estimated from the retina. A person resolves about 30, so this view blurs the picture to 3.95.

A dolphin's eyes sit on the sides of its head. Each sees 120 to 130 degrees to its side, and the two overlap by only 20 to 30 degrees in front. Together that is about 225 degrees, worked out from those figures, and this view squeezes the picture to match.

A bottlenose dolphin sees low light half a log unit better than a person, about three times better, but 0.2 log units worse in bright light. Dolphins, harbour seals and elephant seals have a reflective layer behind the retina. Manatees lack it. We brighten the picture about three times.

Seal whiskers are most sensitive to vibration between 10 and 100 hertz, and a harbour seal can follow a fish's wake for up to 30 seconds after the fish has passed. A phone has no way to give this, so it is left out.

The blur, the squeeze of the field, the brightening, the single colour sensor and the strength of the reflective sheen are the app's choices, set from the records above. A humpback whale's sharpness stands for the whole group, though seals see sharper and manatees see softer. No record gives the strength of the sheen, so it is set by eye.

A bottlenose dolphin sends clicks between 40 and 150 kilohertz, far above what a phone microphone can hear. With the microphone on, the app can draw rings from the sounds it does hear. The drawing is the app's.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a harbor seal, you have one kind of color-sensing cell, where a human has three, and the short-wave kind found in many mammals is missing from your retina. If you are a bowhead or a sperm whale, you have no working cones at all and only rods. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of most other seals, sea lions, whales and dolphins.
rows.note: Left out dolphin/porpoise cone peaks (R3, R11) and the partial manatee table (R13); R2, R4, R12 are dog, pig and deer records and were not used for seals or whales.

rows.title: Some color may remain
rows.text: If you are a sperm whale or a bowhead, the retina of your eye has only rods and no cones, the cells that sense color. If you are a harbor seal, you have no working short-wave color-sensing cell, and a review table lists manatees with two kinds of cone, one short-wave and one long-wave. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of most other species here, sea lions among them.
rows.note: R1 (fox) and R5 (deer) are other species, so I left them out. The R3 quote is cut off, so the sperm whale claim rests on its value field (rod only).

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and every whale, dolphin and seal measured so far sees far less than that. If you are a harbor seal, cell counts in the retina predict about 12 under water, and the same method gives about 4 for a minke whale, a humpback whale or a walrus and about 3 for a bottlenose dolphin. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a sea lion, an elephant seal or a gray whale.
rows.note: Left out killer whale, harp seal and manatee figures for brevity; the killer whale record is PARTIAL (compilation). Fin, blue and other rorquals could be carried from the minke whale but are not named.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: If you are a harbor seal, your eyes held still take in about 210 degrees from side to side, and both eyes see the same part of it over about 65 degrees. If you are a spotted seal, you very likely see about the same, since the harbor seal is a close relative in the same genus. Nobody has measured how wide you see if you are any other whale, dolphin or seal.
rows.note: Only the harbor seal has records for this row. The spotted seal line carries within the genus Phoca. No record supports a human comparison figure for field width, so none is given.

rows.title: Dim light
rows.text: If you are a harbor seal or a California sea lion, your eyes adjust to the dark quickly and end up more sensitive to light than a human's, and if you are a northern elephant seal, you finish adjusting in less than half the time they take. If you are a harp seal, your eyes become close to a hundred million times more sensitive during dark adaptation. Nobody has measured how well you see in dim light if you are a whale, a dolphin, a manatee, or any other seal or sea lion.
rows.note: The row list gives California sea lion grade i, but R4's quote states it was measured, so I named it as measured. Please check the grade. The harp seal figure is 8 log units, written as about a hundred million times.

rows.title: Whiskers
rows.text: If you are a harbor seal, you can wear a blindfold and still follow the trail a miniature submarine left in the water, using only your whiskers. If you are a northern elephant seal, video from wild seals shows you stretch your whiskers forward ahead of your mouth and catch moving prey by the water movement it makes. Nobody has measured this in the other seals and sea lions.
rows.note: Left out the R3 figures (40 m, tens of seconds, 10 to 1,000 Hz): the quote does not name the species and does not state the Hz range.
